title_en: Fragment on the Letter to Philemon
author: Oecumenius
occasion: The fragment comments on Philemon 1:1, explaining why Paul introduces his appeal for Onesimus by mentioning his own imprisonment.
argument: In many letters Paul places an unusual word that prepares for the argument he is about to introduce. Here, because he was about to make a request on behalf of Onesimus, he shows the credibility of his appeal by appealing to his own worth. That worth consists in his being in chains. By mentioning his imprisonment, Paul makes his appeal credible.

outline.move: The commentator explains that Paul's mention of his imprisonment establishes the credibility of his coming appeal for Onesimus.

cast.name: Onesimus
cast.who: The person on whose behalf Paul is about to make a request.

voices.speaker: Oecumenius
voices.how_marked: The entire fragment is the commentator's own explanatory voice.

_unresolved_facts.claim: he shows the credibility of his appeal by appealing to his own worth. That worth consists in his being in chains.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἐπειδὴ ἔμελλεν ἀξιοῦν ὑπὲρ Ὀνησίμου τῇ ἑαυτοῦ ἀξίᾳ– ἀξία δὲ αὐτοῦ τὸ δεδέσθαι–, τὸ ἀξιόπιστον τῆς παρακλήσεως δείκνυσιν
_unresolved_facts.fix: Paul shows the credibility of his appeal by appealing to his own worth/authority (ἀξίᾳ). That worth consists in his being in chains (δεδέσθαι). The commentator states that Paul makes the appeal credible (τὸ ἀξιόπιστον τῆς παρακλήσεως δείκνυσιν), not that Paul makes 'his own appeal' credible in a self-referential sense—the appeal is for Onesimus, and the credibility comes from Paul's imprisoned status.

_unresolved_facts.claim: By mentioning his imprisonment, Paul makes his appeal credible.
_unresolved_facts.fix: Paul shows the credibility of the appeal/entreaty (τῆς παρακλήσεως). The Greek uses a definite article: 'the appeal' (the one he is about to make for Onesimus), not 'his appeal' in a possessive sense. The focus is on the credibility of the supplication itself, which Paul establishes by reference to his chains.
